notes.meaning: Azariah, who is also called Uzziah, became king of Judah while Jeroboam II was ruling in Israel. He began his full, sole rule after having royal duties managed for him during his youth. His name means 'Yahweh has helped,' reminding the people of God's care.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars believe the number twenty-seven was an early scribal copying error for fifteen, to better match the reign dates given in earlier chapters.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early Catholic commentators note that the name Azarias here is likely a copyist variation for Uzziah, who is named directly in the family line of Jesus in the Gospel of Matthew.

notes.meaning: Azariah was sixteen years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for fifty-two years. A godly king enjoying such a long reign brought great stability and peace to the kingdom of Judah. Only King Manasseh ruled longer in Jerusalem.

Azariah did what was right in the eyes of the Lord, following the good start of his father Amaziah. God blessed him with military victory, strong defenses, and national prosperity as long as he sought the Lord.

Even with his good reforms, Azariah failed to take down the high places where the people worshiped. The people continued to offer sacrifices and burn incense on local hills instead of only at God's temple. He lacked the complete zeal needed to wipe out this widespread custom.

The Lord struck Azariah with leprosy, a serious skin disease, because he proudly marched into the temple to burn incense like a priest. By God's law, this made him unclean, so he had to live out his days isolated in a separate house. While the king lived apart, his son Jotham managed the royal palace and governed the people.

The other events and achievements of Azariah's reign were written in the official records of the kings of Judah. Books like Second Chronicles give more details about his successful wars, building projects, and strong army.

When Azariah died, he was buried near his ancestors in the City of David, though kept in an adjoining burial field because of his leprosy. His son Jotham then stepped forward to reign as sole king in his place.

In the thirty-eighth year of Azariah's rule in Judah, Zechariah son of Jeroboam became king of Israel, ruling in Samaria for only six months. His brief reign came after years of confusion and unrest following his father's death.

Zechariah practiced the same evil as his ancestors by keeping up the golden calf worship started by Jeroboam. Even though Israel's kings fought bitterly among themselves, they all agreed on keeping the nation trapped in false worship.

A man named Shallum conspired against Zechariah and struck him down publicly in front of the people. This violent murder ended the royal dynasty of Jehu and revealed how unpopular the king had become.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that early Greek translators mistook the Hebrew phrase for 'before the people' as a proper name, giving rise to theories of a person named Keblaam.

notes.meaning: The rest of Zechariah's short actions were preserved in the royal chronicles of the kings of Israel. Even though he ruled for only half a year, his deeds were carefully noted in the official histories.

Zechariah's death brought about the exact fulfillment of God's promise to Jehu, which said four generations of his descendants would sit on Israel's throne. God remained completely faithful to His word before allowing Jehu's family line to be cut off.
Shallum took the throne in Samaria during the thirty-ninth year of Uzziah, but he held power for only one month. A kingdom that is built on violence and treason rarely stands for very long.

Menahem marched up from the old royal city of Tirzah to Samaria, where he attacked and killed Shallum. He quickly took over the throne, using the very same violence that Shallum had used against his own master.
The rest of what Shallum did and the rebellion he led were recorded in the official chronicles of Israel's kings. His rapid downfall showed that his bloody seizure of power never had God's blessing.

Menahem brutally attacked the city of Tiphsah and all the surrounding territory because its citizens refused to open their gates to him. He even committed the monstrous crime of ripping open pregnant women to terrify anyone who might oppose his rule.

Menahem began his ten-year reign over Israel in the thirty-ninth year of Azariah's rule in Judah. Throughout his whole time on the throne, he continued the same idolatrous calf worship that Jeroboam had introduced to lead the nation into sin.

Pul, the king of Assyria, invaded the land, bringing a serious threat against Israel. Menahem gave him a huge tribute of one thousand talents of silver so that the foreign ruler would support him and secure his grip on the throne.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars identify Pul as the Babylonian throne name of Tiglath-pileser III, whose royal stone inscriptions record taking tribute from King Menahem of Samaria.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic scholars identify Pul with Tiglath-pileser III and suggest that factions within Israel may have invited the Assyrian king into their territory.

notes.meaning: Menahem gathered this silver by taxing the wealthy men of Israel fifty shekels each. Once he received this vast treasure, the king of Assyria withdrew his army and did not stay in the land.
The rest of Menahem's acts were preserved in the royal records of Israel. Unlike most of the northern kings in these final years, Menahem died a natural death, and his son Pekahiah took the throne.
Pekahiah became king of Israel in Azariah's fiftieth year and ruled in Samaria for two years. He lived wickedly in God's sight, refusing to turn away from the idol worship of Jeroboam.

Pekah, an officer in the king's army, formed a plot against Pekahiah with fifty men from Gilead. They broke into the inner fortress of the palace in Samaria, struck down the king and his loyal officers, and Pekah made himself ruler.
The other events of Pekahiah's short reign were written down in the chronicles of Israel's kings. His early death showed that Israel remained in deep moral decay and political chaos.

Pekah took the throne of Israel in the final year of Azariah's reign in Judah and ruled in Samaria for twenty years. Even with another change of leadership, he continued the same evil calf-worship as the rulers before him.

During Pekah's reign, Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria invaded northern Israel and captured many fortified cities across Galilee and Gilead. He carried the people away as captives to Assyria, which fulfilled earlier warnings of judgment against Israel's idolatry.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note that Tiglath-pileser's royal annals discovered at Nimrud describe this western invasion, though the specific names of some smaller towns are not fully preserved.

notes.meaning: Hoshea plotted against Pekah, murdered him, and took over the throne of Israel. This takeover happened twenty years after Jotham began to reign in Judah, continuing the violent cycle of assassinations in the north.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note the difficulty of this date since Jotham ruled sixteen years, and they often explain it as counting from the start of Jotham's rule into the reign of his son Ahaz, or as an early copying difficulty.

notes.meaning: The rest of Pekah's accomplishments and wars were written in the official annals of the kings of Israel. Though he reigned for two decades and fought major wars, his reign ended in the same bloodshed that started it.

Jotham son of Uzziah began his sole reign over Judah in the second year of Pekah's rule in Israel. He was twenty-five years old when he started ruling alone, and he reigned for sixteen years in Jerusalem after having served as his father's deputy during the years of leprosy.

Jotham did what was right in the eyes of the Lord, following the good pattern set by his father Uzziah. Unlike his father, however, he did not sin by pridefully trespassing into the temple sanctuary to offer incense.

Even with Jotham's good character, the high places remained, and the people continued to burn sacrifices and incense there. Jotham showed his honor for God by rebuilding the Upper Gate that led into the temple court.
The rest of Jotham's deeds were written in the chronicles of the kings of Judah. Second Chronicles tells how he strengthened Judah's fortifications and defeated the Ammonites in battle.

Near the end of Jotham's life, the Lord began sending King Rezin of Aram and King Pekah of Israel against Judah. Although these enemies acted out of selfish political ambition, God used them as His rod of discipline against Judah's sins.
Jotham died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David. His son Ahaz took the throne after him, beginning a troubled period of deep idolatry for the kingdom of Judah.
